newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rebels take town, cut Zaire rail route-expatriates.
newsitem.headline: Rebels take town, cut Zaire rail route-expatriates.

text.p: Rebels have taken the town of Kamina, severing a vital rail supply route into Zaire's diamond-rich Kasai province, expatriate sources said on Monday.
The sources, in contact with Kamina until late Monday morning, said Laurent Kabila's rebel forces appeared to have headed down from the north-east, many of them by foot, and taken the town overnight.
"There was no battle for the city and no looting," said one source in Lubumbashi, the capital of Shaba province in the far south-east copperbelt and one of Kabila's next declared targets.
The news sent a shiver of apprehension through Lubumbashi, which remains calm in the face of fresh rebel advances.
Kamina is 600 km (400 miles) northwest of Lubumbashi, 24 hours away by train along the line that runs up into Kasai province and down to Shaba, Zambia and South Africa.
A Belgian-South African consortium has been running the railway for two years, before which much-needed food and other supplies only reached Kasai in bulk by air.
Rail officials said Kamina was a centre for rolling stock.
The rebels were previously believed to have access only to one old locomotive taken in the eastern lake port of Kalemie.
Local expatriates speculated that they might be able to speed their advance on Lubumbashi and north towards the Kasai capital Mbuji-Mayi if they managed to use the trains.
Zaire's military had a major army and airforce base some 25 km (15 miles) outside Kamina, though in recent weeks locals reported it was largely deserted.
The air base was reputedly used in the 1970s by the United States to support Angola's UNITA rebels.
It was unclear on Monday how many Zairean troops were in the Kamina area, or if they were on the move.

Rebels also claim to be in possession of Kasenga, a small town only 220 km (130 miles) northeast of Lubumbashi, as they approach the city from different directions. Zaire's army chief of staff has denied the claim.
The rebels took up arms in October, vowing to topple President Mobutu Sese Seko, who was in Europe at the time recuperating after prostate cancer surgery.

Many ordinary Zaireans, hungry for change from the poverty they have suffered under three decades of Mobutu rule, have been openly rallying to Kabila. The rebels now hold a quarter of the sprawling Central African nation.
Shaba and Kasai are crucial to the economy of Zaire, which is potentially one of Africa's richest countries but has been impoverished by official corruption and administrative chaos.
Shaba's mines are a potentially lucrative source of wealth and have attracted many expatriates, mainly Belgian, to the area. Most are still in the area but have sent families away.
